items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Panel remarks at the 2026 ASSA Annual Meeting, 'Thoughts on the U.S. Economy and the Year Ahead'
items.quote: If all of that happens, then some modest further adjustments to the funds rate would likely be appropriate later in the year.
items.summary: Paulson said she is cautiously optimistic on inflation, expecting the tariff price-level shift to run its course in the first half and run-rate inflation near 2 percent by year end. She views the funds rate as still a little restrictive and said the trends argue against tighter policy. The labor market is bending but not breaking, and if inflation moderates and the labor market stabilizes, modest further cuts later in the year would be appropriate. She discussed AI-driven productivity as a possible reason for strong GDP with weak hiring.
items.score_note: Policy still a little restrictive, labor risks elevated, modest further cuts later in the year in her baseline; no urgency, so -1 not -2.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Council on Foreign Relations, New York, 'A Few Words for the New Year'
items.quote: Monetary policy is now well positioned to support the stabilization of the labor market and the return of inflation to the FOMC’s longer-run goal of 2 percent.
items.summary: Williams said the 75 bp of cuts in 2025 moved a modestly restrictive stance closer to neutral and brought risks into better balance. He expects inflation to peak at about 2-3/4 to 3 percent in the first half of 2026 as tariffs pass through, then fall to 2 percent in 2027, with GDP growth of 2-1/2 to 2-3/4 percent. He gave no signal on timing of further moves and said he remains data dependent; reserve management purchases are not a change in stance. Speaking to reporters afterward, he warned that attacks on central bank independence often lead to bad outcomes including high inflation, and said he hoped the next chair would uphold the dual mandate.
items.score_note: Describes policy as well positioned after the 2025 cuts with no lean on the next move; balanced hold.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia State of the Economy event, 'Economic Trends and Opportunities for Philadelphia'
items.quote: I view the current level of the federal funds rate as still a little restrictive.
items.summary: Paulson repeated her ASSA message: cautious optimism on inflation (December CPI did not change her view), the funds rate still a little restrictive, and trends that argue against tighter policy. Labor market risks have risen though claims are flat. If inflation moderates, the labor market stabilizes and growth is around 2 percent, some modest further adjustments to the funds rate would likely be appropriate later in the year.
items.score_note: Same easing lean as January 3: restrictive policy, labor risks, modest cuts later in the year conditional on the baseline.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Wall Street Journal interview (published January 15; highlights as relayed by investingLive)
items.quote: comfortable holding interest rates steady
items.summary: Paulson told the WSJ she is comfortable holding rates steady at the January 27-28 meeting and sees no hurry to cut again. She views the current range as slightly above neutral and wants to see January price data. She said labor market risks are a little bit higher than inflation risks and that the labor market could break quickly; she could favor modest cuts later in the year if inflation falls as she expects or the labor market weakens. The WSJ original is paywalled; only short quoted phrases are available in the open summary.
items.score_note: Supports a January hold, but sees policy above neutral, labor risks slightly higher than inflation risks, and modest cuts later in the year; easing lean without urgency.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech to the Ohio Bankers League, 'Recipe for a Thriving US Economy: Strong Banks, Patient Policy, and an Independent yet Accountable Central Bank'
items.quote: Based on my forecast, we could be on hold for quite some time.
items.summary: Hammack said she supported the January hold, that the funds rate is in the vicinity of neutral and not meaningfully restraining the economy, and that she prefers to err on the side of patience rather than fine tune. Inflation is still too high and has moved sideways for two years, with a risk it stays near 3 percent. She sees the risks of a higher or lower path for the funds rate as about balanced and defended Fed independence. In the banking half of the speech she listed nonbank growth, including private credit, among the well-known financial-stability risks.
items.score_note: Extended hold with explicitly balanced risks to the rate path; pushes back on near-term cuts but states no tightening lean. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.ai_quote: These services include private credit, whose speed, flexibility, limited disclosure, and customization often make it an appealing alternative to traditional bank loans.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Moderated conversation with the Ohio State University community at WOSU Public Media, Columbus (as reported by The Lantern)
items.quote: I think we’re supposed to stay on hold right here
items.summary: At a mostly educational event about how the Fed works, Hammack said the labor market is stabilizing and that keeping rates where they are is the right course to bring inflation down; she does not want to fine-tune the economy. MNI separately reported that on February 11 she said the January jobs report showed a labor market finding a healthy balance while inflation is still too high.
items.score_note: Restates the hold from her February 10 speech with no new lean; student-newspaper report with a short direct quote.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at America's Credit Unions Governmental Affairs Conference, Washington DC, 'Two Sides of a Coin'
items.quote: further reductions in the federal funds rate will eventually be warranted to prevent monetary policy from inadvertently becoming more restrictive
items.summary: Williams said policy is well positioned, tariff effects on prices look one-off with no second-round effects, and inflation should fall to about 2-1/2 percent in 2026 and 2 percent in 2027. If inflation follows that path, further rate reductions will eventually be warranted so that policy does not passively tighten. He expects GDP growth of about 2-1/2 percent and unemployment edging down. The prepared text did not mention the Iran war; in comments the same day reported by MNI he said it was early days, that higher energy prices affect the near-term inflation outlook, and that the shock can hit both mandate goals in opposing ways.
items.score_note: No urgency (policy 'well positioned' now), but he explicitly states an easing bias: further cuts eventually warranted if inflation falls as he expects.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: New York Times interview (published March 4; quotes as relayed by Reuters)
items.quote: It’s important to make sure that we’re maintaining policy at a level where we can drive inflation back down to target while balancing any potential softness in the labor market
items.summary: Hammack said it is too early to gauge the economic impact of the Iran war and backed holding rates steady for quite some time. With inflation too high and the labor market relatively steady, the Fed should stay focused on price pressures. She laid out both directions: more accommodation if the labor market weakens further, more restriction if inflation does not move toward target as she expects.
items.score_note: Extended hold with both a cut and a hike scenario spelled out; emphasis on inflation but no lean on the next move.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Discussant remarks at the 2026 US Monetary Policy Forum on 'Private Canaries: The Value of Private-Sector Data for U.S. Monetary Policy Making'
items.quote: Private data and public data are complements.
items.summary: Paulson discussed how the FOMC assembles a picture of the economy from public and private data and how data use may explain gaps between policymaker and market rate expectations. She suggested communication could be improved by being systematic about which data matter and why. She gave no view on the current stance or rate path.
items.score_note: Discussion of data and communication; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Panel remarks at the 2026 US Monetary Policy Forum (Chicago Booth, New York), 'On the Safe-Haven Status of the Dollar'
items.quote: Under my base case, I think policy should be on hold for quite some time as we see evidence that inflation is coming down and the labor market stabilizes further.
items.summary: In remarks mostly about the dollar's reserve role, Hammack said policy is in a good position with the funds rate around neutral. Her base case is an extended hold while inflation comes down and the labor market stabilizes, and she sees two-sided risks to rates. She also flagged the unsustainable path of US fiscal debt as a risk to demand for dollar assets and stressed Fed independence.
items.score_note: Extended hold with two-sided risks to rates; no lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Reuters interview (New York, same day as her US Monetary Policy Forum remarks)
items.quote: that might be a reason why we might need to be more restrictive from policy perspective
items.summary: On the day February payrolls fell by 92,000 and markets added to rate-cut bets, Hammack said rates should be on hold for quite some time and that she still expects decent progress on inflation this year. If inflation is not making progress in the second half, the Fed might need to be more restrictive. She said it is too early to judge the oil shock, which depends on its magnitude and persistence, and that the jobs data show signs of stabilizing.
items.score_note: Base case is hold, but the only conditional she raised was tightening and she played down the weak jobs report; open to hiking. Her same-day prepared remarks (scored 0) cite two-sided risks, so this is a mild +1.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Macroeconomics and Monetary Policy Conference (San Francisco Fed), 'Monetary Policy and Productivity'
items.quote: But if inflation is above 2 percent and has been for some time, I would be more cautious.
items.summary: Paulson laid out low, medium and high productivity scenarios for AI and their implications for the long-run funds rate. She said the 1990s Greenspan-style patience relied on credibility earned with inflation at 2 percent, whereas inflation has now been above target for six years, is 2.8 percent, and the Middle East conflict adds risks to inflation and growth. Faced with a growth surge she would weight the possibility of overheating more heavily; she sees no sign the labor market is adding to inflation. In the Q&A (Reuters, MNI) she said she is worried that repeated supply shocks pass more quickly and durably into inflation expectations, while calling the labor market fragile and stressing risks to both inflation and growth.
items.score_note: Conditional, hypothetical lean toward caution on inflation but no statement on the next move; between 0 and +1, chose 0. Earlier 'cuts later this year' language is absent.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Staten Island Economic Development Corporation, 'Ferrying Through the Crosscurrents'
items.quote: But the current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to balance the risks to our maximum employment and price stability goals.
items.summary: Williams said the Middle East conflict has pushed up energy prices and could become a large supply shock that raises inflation and dampens activity, on top of tariffs; PCE inflation is around 3 percent. Longer-term expectations remain anchored and there are no second-round tariff effects. He called the stance well positioned to balance risks, raised his 2026 inflation forecast to about 2-3/4 percent, and dropped the earlier language about eventual further reductions. He told reporters that uncertainties and risks to both goals have increased and that he is using energy market pricing as his guide while watching for other scenarios.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks and 'well positioned'; no easing-bias sentence this time and no tightening lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Associated Press interview
items.quote: Or I could see where we might need to raise rates if inflation stays persistently above our target.
items.summary: Hammack told the AP her preference is to keep rates unchanged for quite some time, but she can foresee cutting if the labor market deteriorates significantly or raising rates if inflation stays persistently above target. Cleveland Fed estimates show inflation could reach 3.5 percent in April, which she described as moving in the wrong direction. Gas prices are the top concern she hears in her district, and the war has already lasted longer than she expected at the March meeting.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided (cut and hike scenarios) around an extended hold. Between 0 and +1 given the stress on inflation; chose 0.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: NPR 'The Indicator from Planet Money' podcast, joint interview with Austan Goolsbee (taped April 1, reported April 6)
items.quote: We've been trading closer to 3% than our objective of 2%.
items.summary: Asked to rate the economy by color, Hammack put inflation at a bright orange: above target for about five years and basically moving sideways for the past two. She rated the labor market yellow-green, with unemployment right around her estimate of maximum employment though in a fragile low-hiring, low-firing balance. She called financial stability generally green, naming private credit as a pocket she is watching and noting that financial conditions tightened over the past month. The transcript has no explicit rate-path comment; Reuters characterized both officials as seeing inflation as a far bigger problem than employment.
items.score_note: No rate-path statement; inflation risk clearly dominates labor in her own assessment, which is the +1 definition. Weak evidence, so treat as a soft +1. Taped before the March jobs report.
items.ai_quote: Private credit is certainly one of them.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview
items.quote: I expect headline inflation to actually be elevated, you know, in the middle of this year
items.summary: Williams said the Middle East energy shock will feed directly into headline inflation, which he expects to be elevated mid-year and about 2.75 percent for 2026, while reiterating that monetary policy is in the right place. Per MNI's transcript of the same interview he called policy 'really well positioned' to wait and see, kept his core inflation view near 2.5 percent, and trimmed his growth forecast to 2 to 2.5 percent. He also said FOMC leadership continuity is not in question if Warsh's confirmation is delayed.
items.score_note: Wait-and-see hold; acknowledges higher headline inflation but no change in his view of underlying inflation and no lean on the next move.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: CNBC interview
items.quote: My baseline is that we’re going to remain on hold for a good while, but I do think that there’s two-sided risk to rates
items.summary: Hammack said rates are in a good place and her baseline is an extended hold, with risk that policy may need to be either more accommodative or more restrictive depending on the data. The key question is how high energy prices stay and for how long. She cautioned that successive supply shocks on top of already elevated inflation may not be something the Fed can look through, and said it is a good time to stay patient.
items.score_note: Hold with explicitly two-sided rate risk; the caution about looking through supply shocks is not yet a lean.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York 2026 Member Symposium, 'The Cosmos'
items.quote: This is an unusual set of circumstances, but the current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to balance the risks to our maximum employment and price stability goals.
items.summary: Williams repeated that the stance is well positioned as the Middle East conflict raises energy prices and risks a broader supply shock. He expects 2026 inflation of 2-3/4 to 3 percent, GDP growth of 2 to 2-1/2 percent and unemployment in a 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent range, with inflation back at 2 percent in 2027. Short-term inflation expectations have risen but medium and longer-term ones remain anchored. He also described the ample reserves framework as working well. He told reporters inflation will be well above 3 percent over the next few months, that it is not a time for strong forward guidance, and that it will be appropriate to bring rates down if inflation moderates back to 2 percent, 'but that's not where we are today'.
items.score_note: Balanced hold; flags both inflation and activity risks from the energy shock without a lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: FOMC statement, April 28-29 meeting: dissent against retaining the easing bias (with Kashkari and Logan)
items.quote: who supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time
items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3.50-3.75 percent by an 8-4 vote. Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissented: they supported the hold but opposed keeping the 'additional adjustments' easing-bias language in the statement. Miran dissented in favor of a 25 bp cut. The quote is the statement's vote line, not Hammack's own words.
items.score_note: Hawkish dissent on forward guidance (remove easing bias) while supporting the hold; not a vote for a hike, so +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Statement regarding her vote at the April 28-29 FOMC meeting
items.quote: I see this clear easing bias as no longer appropriate given the outlook.
items.summary: Hammack explained that she supported holding the funds rate steady but dissented because the statement's 'additional adjustments' language signals a pause in an easing cycle. She said inflation pressures are broad based, rising oil prices add to them, and unemployment has been near her estimate of full employment since last summer. She sees upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth and employment.
items.score_note: Wants the easing bias removed because of inflation risks; supports hold and does not call for a hike.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Cynosure Group Spring Symposium, New York, 'There Is No Try'
items.quote: Right now, the future is difficult to see, and the risks to both sides of our mandate have increased.
items.summary: Williams said PCE inflation rose to 3-1/2 percent in March, with tariffs and energy adding about a percentage point, and that he expects about 3 percent for 2026 before a return to 2 percent in 2027. He said the stance is well positioned to balance the risks and noted last week's FOMC hold at 3.50-3.75 percent. Risks to both sides of the mandate have increased and several plausible Middle East scenarios involve more severe supply dislocations. He told reporters he cannot give strong guidance for the next several meetings, sees nothing in the data that calls for a hike in the near term, fully supports the statement's language, and still expects cuts at some point once inflation falls, with the date pushed back.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate with risks higher on both sides; no directional lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: WOSU public radio interview (Columbus, Ohio)
items.quote: I think our statement should have a pretty neutral stance about whether the next move is down or up or just on hold for a really long period of time
items.summary: Hammack said her outlook is that rates will be on hold for quite some time and explained her April dissent: the statement should be neutral about whether the next move is down, up, or a long hold. She played down the discord implied by the 8-4 vote. Inflation has missed 2 percent for five years and the Iran conflict could make price pressures more persistent, while the job market is stable and inflation expectations are largely anchored.
items.score_note: Repeats the case for dropping the easing bias because inflation may be more persistent; her own desired stance is 'neutral', so this is +1 only in the sense of pushing back on cut guidance (consistent with the May 1 statement).

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the Ohio CEO Summit, Columbus
items.quote: What I hear when I’m out with businesses is I hear concern that an inflationary mindset is starting to become entrenched in people’s minds
items.summary: Hammack said a series of shocks, from COVID-19 to Russia's invasion of Ukraine to the Iran war, has kept inflation above 2 percent for more than five years, and businesses tell her an inflationary mindset is starting to become entrenched. Reuters reported she said the Fed needs to keep an open mind about its next policy move.
items.score_note: Inflation-expectations risk dominates her remarks a week after dissenting against the easing bias; no explicit call to hike.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at a Conference of Business Economists event, New York
items.quote: I don’t see there’s any reason at all to raise rates right now or lower rates right now
items.summary: Williams said monetary policy is in a good place and he sees no reason to raise or lower rates now, despite the Middle East energy shock and a jump in April CPI. Short-term inflation expectations have risen but longer-term ones are stable, the labor market is not adding to price pressures, and he sees no unusual second-round effects so far. He said the strong stock market reflects optimism about AI-related productivity growth.
items.score_note: Explicitly rules out both a hike and a cut for now; balanced hold on a day when markets were adding hike bets.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Atlanta Fed 2026 Financial Markets Conference, 'Navigating Uncertainty: Inflation, Labor Markets, and the Stance of Monetary Policy'
items.quote: Assuming the labor market remains in balance, rate cuts would only become appropriate once we have seen sustained progress on inflation.
items.summary: Paulson said inflation is too high (headline PCE 3.5 percent, core 3.2 percent in March) because of tariffs and the Middle East energy shock, but policy is mildly restrictive and appropriately positioned. Keeping rates steady lets the Fed assess risks; cuts need sustained inflation progress. She called it healthy that markets now price scenarios of an extended hold or further tightening, and said tightening might be needed if inflation expectations slip. She cited solid growth bolstered by AI infrastructure investment. In post-speech comments reported by MNI she said she did not join the April dissents because she saw no communication problem to solve, as markets had already priced out cuts.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate; rules out near-term cuts and accepts tightening scenarios, but describes policy as already mildly restrictive and well positioned. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland, 'Productivity Growth and the Challenge of Real-Time Policymaking'
items.quote: Second, an increase in trend productivity growth raises real interest rates in the long run.
items.summary: A research-style speech on how shifts in trend productivity growth affect the economy and real interest rates, using historical episodes and model simulations. Williams avoided speculating on AI and gave no comment on the current stance or near-term rate path. He concluded that structural shifts are hard to identify in real time, which favors robust policy approaches.
items.score_note: No statement on the current policy stance or rate path; conceptual discussion only.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Q&A at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland (after his productivity speech)
items.quote: Right now monetary policy for the Fed is, is right where we want it to be
items.summary: In the discussion after his prepared speech, Williams said policy is slightly restrictive and well positioned to keep learning about the conflict and the data before any decision. He expects PCE inflation close to 4 percent and core above 3 percent over the next few months, easing as tariff and energy effects fade. Asked about hikes, he said persistently high inflation or rising long-term expectations would call for somewhat higher real rates, but that is not where things are today (per Reuters and MNI accounts).
items.score_note: Policy 'right where we want it'; names the condition for a hike but says it is not the current outlook. Separate item from the prepared text because the speech itself has no stance.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks to a business group in New Jersey (as reported by Reuters)
items.quote: as well as scenarios where further tightening becomes necessary
items.summary: Paulson said monetary policy is well positioned given unacceptably high inflation and economic uncertainty, and that the Fed is ready to react. She repeated that it is healthy that markets have taken on board scenarios in which the funds rate stays unchanged for an extended period as well as scenarios where further tightening becomes necessary. No official text was posted on the Philadelphia Fed site.
items.score_note: Same message as her May 19 speech: policy in the right place, open to both an extended hold and tightening scenarios. Between 0 and +1; chose 0.

coverage_notes: Official texts: every Williams entry on the New York Fed speeches page dated January to May 2026 was opened (Jan 12, Mar 3, Mar 30, Apr 16, May 4, May 28); the Teller Window blog has only 'key takeaways' posts for those speeches in the window. Every Hammack entry in the Cleveland Fed speeches collection was opened (Feb 10, Mar 6, May 1 statement) and every Paulson entry on the Philadelphia Fed speeches-and-essays page (Jan 3 x2, Jan 14, Mar 6, Mar 27, Apr 14, May 19). Dissents: the January 28, March 18 and April 29 FOMC statements were opened. January: Miran and Waller dissented for a cut; March: Miran. Williams, Hammack and Paulson voted with the majority at both. April 29 was 8-4: Miran for a cut, and Hammack, Kashkari and Logan against keeping the easing bias while supporting the hold. Hammack published a statement on May 1 (in the Cleveland Fed speeches collection). The brief's context mentions only Logan's May 1 statement; Hammack's and (per Reuters) Kashkari's exist too. Williams and Paulson did not dissent in the window. The April 29 dissent item quotes the FOMC statement's vote line, which is not Hammack's own words; her own words are in the May 1 statement item. Wire remarks: found through the SRN News archive (Reuters reprints, queried via its WordPress API), MNI's public inter-meeting Fed-speak compilations (January 22, March 12, April 23, June 11 editions) and Google News title scans by speaker and month. Sources used for quotes besides official pages: SRN News (Reuters), PBS (AP), NPR transcript, The Lantern (Ohio State student paper), investingLive (summary of a paywalled WSJ interview; only short quoted phrases). Where a speech has an official text and reporters' Q&A added to it, the Q&A is folded into that item's summary (Williams Jan 12, Mar 3, Mar 30, Apr 16, May 4; Paulson Mar 27, May 19). Exception: Williams May 28 has two items, the prepared productivity speech (no stance, score null) and the Q&A where he gave his stance. Thin months, which look genuine rather than missed: Williams has nothing in February and nothing between January 13 and March 2 (MNI's March compilation also lists only March 3 for him). Hammack has nothing in January (MNI's January 22 compilation shows her last remarks as December 12) and nothing between March 7 and April 5 or after May 7 until her June 2 speech. Paulson has nothing in February or April with monetary-policy content (MNI: 'No commentary on current monetary policy since last FOMC meeting' as of March 12; April 14 was a rural-investment fireside chat with video only) and her May 29 remarks are known only from one Reuters roundup paragraph. Blackout periods (roughly Jan 17-29, Mar 7-19, Apr 18-30) explain part of the gaps. Date notes: Hammack's NYT interview is dated by publication (March 4); the NPR podcast was taped April 1 and published April 6; Reuters' April 16 story calls her CNBC interview 'Tuesday' but Reuters' own April 15 story and CNBC date it Wednesday April 15, which is used. MNI calls Williams's 'The Cosmos' speech April 17; the New York Fed page and Reuters say April 16. A Google News listing dated 'May 11' for 'Hammack: gradual rate hikes' (investingLive, FXStreet) is a misdated November 5 story and was excluded. ai_financing is tagged on two Hammack items only because she named private credit as a financial-stability risk (Feb 10 speech, April 6 podcast); neither links it to AI capex or to the rate path. Williams and Paulson mention AI investment only as a growth driver, which was not tagged. time_et is filled only where the source page states a time (Hammack's two speeches, the FOMC statement). Context check: nothing opened contradicts the brief's context section; the FOMC statements confirm the 3.50-3.75 percent range at all three meetings, Reuters headlines in the SRN archive date Warsh's nomination to January 30 and his Senate confirmation to May 13, and AP and Reuters describe a US-Israel war with Iran from February 28 as the source of the energy shock (not mentioned in the brief).
